criterion_notes.c1: Examines urban and peri-urban household and community water service access in Senegal and Burkina Faso, specifically residential piped water connection rates, standpipe connections, overall service coverage, and subsidised social water connections.
criterion_notes.c2: Passes BOTH the plain wording of Criterion 2 and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading. Under the plain wording, it examines statutory, regulatory, contractual, and governance reforms in urban water utilities (Senegalese Law No. 95-10, 30-year concession, 10-year affermage/lease, and performance contracts in Senegal and Burkina Faso). Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, it directly analyzes utility ownership and regulatory structure governing service access (separation of state Asset Owner Company SONES with a statutory social/solidarity purpose from private operator SDE, and public corporatized utility ONEA under performance contracts) together with tariff, cost-recovery, and connection rules (3% annual tariff increase cap, subsidised social volume under 20 m3 per 2-month period for low-income households, risk-sharing remuneration formulas, and contractual social water connection targets).
criterion_notes.c3: Although Sections 1-3 develop a formal microeconomic incomplete-contract model, Section 4 presents an empirical comparative institutional case study of SONES/SDE in Senegal (1996-2013) and ONEA in Burkina Faso (2002-2011) based on explicit case selection, longitudinal utility administrative data (1996-2013 and annual 1996-2011/2000-2011 series), primary statutory and contractual provisions, and an interview/contacts with utility officials (including an April 26, 2013 interview with M. Dia of SDE). Lack of an econometric effect estimate does not exclude an institutional/socio-legal case study from the review under Criteria 3 and 6.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports concrete access and affordability outcomes at the utility/population level, including urban service coverage (80% to 98.70% in Senegal), access to piped water through residential connections (58% to 88.50% in Senegal; 54% to 80% in Burkina Faso), standpipe connections (22% to 10.20%), total water connections (241,167 to 581,422 in Senegal; 67,207 to 210,720 in Burkina Faso), cumulative/annual social connections (3,299 in 1996 to 163,143 in 2011), and subsidised social tariff rules.
criterion_notes.c5: Population and unit of analysis (national urban/peri-urban water utilities SONES/SDE in Senegal and ONEA in Burkina Faso and their served urban populations), exposure (1995 statutory creation of Asset Owner Company SONES, 30-year concession, 10-year affermage and performance contracts, risk-sharing remuneration formula, tariff cap, and social connection/social volume rules; 3-year performance-based service contract at ONEA), outcome (service coverage, residential piped access, total and social connections), and study design (formal incomplete-contract model paired with longitudinal comparative institutional utility case studies) are all identifiable.

evidence_quotes.quote: Between 1996 and 2013, access to water piped through residential connections increased by over 50 %, while network yield grew by over 17 % in the same period.

SONES owns the water service assets under the terms of a 30-year concession contract with the Senegalese government. SDE operates the system and provides water services under a 10-year affermage contract with SONES.

The aim of the entity must include one or more social purposes: a high level of infrastructure investment and ﬁnancial equilibrium without major tariff increase (limited to 3 % per year), lowest price per m3, and a program of social water access connections carried out between 1996 and 2011 (Fig. 4).

The contract also deﬁnes a gradual increase in tariffs over time, adjusted according to progress in reaching ﬁnancial equilibrium, and a subsidised ‘‘social volume’’ for consumption of under 20 cubic meters per 2-months period for low-income households.

In conjunction with the government, ONEA worked within the framework of 3-year performance contracts with explicit operational targets. We selected these cases due to the availability of data and contacts with ofﬁcials in these entities.

As Table 3, Figs. 2 and 3 illustrate, SDE’s transformation is remarkable. From 1996 to 2013, its production capacity increased by 60 % to 118 million cubic meters. Likewise, its service coverage increased by 23 %. The number of residents with piped water connections has increased by 50 %.

raw_response.exposure: Utility ownership, regulatory, and contractual structure reforms: Senegalese Law No. 95-10 establishing an Asset Owner Company (SONES) with a solidarity purpose under a 30-year state concession, a 10-year affermage (lease) and performance contract with private operator SDE featuring risk-sharing volumetric remuneration, a 3% annual tariff increase cap, a subsidised social tariff block (<20 m3 per 2 months for low-income households), and a social connections program; and 3-year performance-based service contracts between the state and public utility ONEA in Burkina Faso.
raw_response.outcome: Urban and peri-urban water service coverage (%), residential piped water connection access (%), standpipe connection share (%), total number of connections, number of subsidised social water connections (1996-2011), water production and sales volume, biological water quality conformity (%), and customer bill payment rate (%).
raw_response.population_and_sample: Urban and peri-urban water utilities and served populations in two Sub-Saharan African countries: SONES and Sénégalaise des Eaux (SDE) in Senegal (1996-2013; growing from 241,167 to 581,422 connections) and Office National de l'Eau et de l'Assainissement (ONEA) in Burkina Faso (2002-2011; growing from 67,207 to 210,720 connections). Unit of analysis: water utility.
raw_response.rationale: Nakhla (2016) satisfies all systematic-review inclusion criteria under both the plain reading and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2. While the first half of the article develops a formal incomplete-contract model with financing constraints, Section 4 presents a comparative longitudinal institutional case study of urban water utility reforms in Senegal (SONES/SDE, 1996-2013) and Burkina Faso (ONEA, 2002-2011) drawing on utility administrative time-series data, statutory and contract provisions (Senegalese Law No. 95-10, concession, affermage, and performance contracts), and official interview/utility contacts. It directly examines rule-type ownership, contractual, and tariff mechanisms governing household water access (Asset Owner Company separation, risk-sharing lease remuneration formulas, 3% tariff increase caps, subsidised social volume blocks under 20 m3 per 2 months, and social connection programs) and reports concrete utility-level outcomes on service coverage, residential piped connections, standpipe share, and social connections. Confidence is medium because the empirical case analysis serves primarily to illustrate the theoretical model with descriptive pre-post/time-series utility statistics rather than an independent causal identification design, though Criterion 6 statistical synthesis requirements do not restrict systematic-review inclusion.
raw_response.study_design: Formal incomplete-contract theoretical model combined with a comparative longitudinal institutional case study (descriptive before-and-after/time-series utility administrative data, statutory/contractual analysis, and official interview).
